name: Rotate to Carni
description: Rotating to Carni seeks a leg-assisted shoulder clamp after clearing the high leg around the head and turning partly belly down with triceps and wrist control.
summary: Rotating to Carni seeks a leg-assisted shoulder clamp after clearing the high leg around the head and turning partly belly down with triceps and wrist control.
overview:
The bottom guard player begins in New York with a safe neck-clearing angle, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Richie Martinez demonstrates the shoulder-lock mechanics through Jersey from Z guard. A direct New York entry is a positional adaptation, not established by that lesson alone.

Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head. Turn partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported rather than wrenching the leg across the head.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Richie Martinez — Carni shoulder lock from Z guard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iClQ2Np-n30).

attacker.description: Rotate to Carni (attacker): Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head.
attacker.overview:
The bottom guard player begins in New York with a safe neck-clearing angle, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Richie Martinez demonstrates the shoulder-lock mechanics through Jersey from Z guard. A direct New York entry is a positional adaptation, not established by that lesson alone.

Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head. Turn partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported rather than wrenching the leg across the head.

Keep the captured arm connected so the opponent cannot freely roll or withdraw the shoulder. Hold the wrist and elbow at a comfortable angle; a small change can load the shoulder rapidly. Release the wrist and leg clamp immediately on a tap or when the partner needs to roll safely.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Hip movement turns the supported knee and torso into the shoulder clamp while the neck frame blocks forward chest pressure. Carni is a rotational lock and a new submission entry: the triceps connection must prevent the arm withdrawing before any finishing angle is considered.

Anchor through the hips: Turn partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported rather than wrenching the leg across the head.
Hold the triceps: Keep the captured arm connected so the opponent cannot freely roll or withdraw the shoulder.
Control before finishing: Hold the wrist and elbow at a comfortable angle; a small change can load the shoulder rapidly.
Let the lock go: Release the wrist and leg clamp immediately on a tap or when the partner needs to roll safely.

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): What should be close before you clear the high leg?
flashcards.answer: Bring the opponent close through the guard and shoulder connection before moving the head-side leg.
flashcards.answer_line: The opponent's shoulder connected to your guard

plausible: Only the wrist while the shoulder stays distant
Their chest upright beyond your supported knee
trap: Their head close while the target arm remains free

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): What preserves space as the leg travels around the head?
flashcards.answer: The neck-side forearm frame manages incoming chest pressure while the high leg clears.
flashcards.answer_line: An inside forearm at the side of the neck

plausible: A wrist outside the incoming chest
Both hands pulling the raised foot
trap: A straight-arm pull on the captured wrist

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): Which torso angle helps anchor the shoulder clamp?
flashcards.answer: The shown Carni angle combines a partial belly-down turn, a close knee and a supported foot.
flashcards.answer_line: Partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported

plausible: Flat on the back with the knee wide
Fully upright with the high foot floating
trap: Facing away with the captured arm stretched behind you

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): What stops the opponent freely rolling out of the shoulder clamp?
flashcards.answer: Martinez retains the triceps so the arm cannot simply withdraw or roll freely from the clamp.
flashcards.answer_line: Retention of the upper arm through triceps control

plausible: Only wrist control with the upper arm free
Only the neck-side frame after releasing the arm
trap: Only the supported foot while the elbow slips out

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): What should be checked before any wrist leverage is added?
flashcards.answer: Verify the supported capture without finishing pressure; small wrist-and-elbow changes can load the fixed shoulder.
flashcards.answer_line: The arm is captured at a comfortable shoulder angle

plausible: Only that the wrist can be moved farther
Only that the head-side foot has reached the mat
trap: Only that the lower butterfly hook remains

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): Which connections must open when the partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Release wrist leverage and the leg clamp immediately so the shoulder can move freely.
flashcards.answer_line: The wrist grip and shoulder-clamping leg

plausible: Only the wrist grip while the leg keeps clamping
Only the leg clamp while the wrist remains leveraged
trap: Only finishing pressure while both controls remain closed

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): What arm relationship should exist in the described New York start?
flashcards.answer: The described entry begins with New York arm isolation and a comfortable neck-clearing angle; its direct Carni route remains conditional.
flashcards.answer_line: An isolated opposing arm linked to the knee hug

plausible: Both opposing arms still free inside the high clinch
The target hand on the mat with the knee hug open
trap: The target wrist outside while its elbow returns inside

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): What must be added after head clearance to establish the shoulder lock?
flashcards.answer: Clearing the head alone is not the shoulder lock; establish the upper-arm connection and supported Carni angle separately.
flashcards.answer_line: A retained upper arm in the new shoulder clamp

plausible: A wrist grip while the upper arm stays free
A supported foot with the elbow already outside
trap: A tighter head grip with no triceps retention

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): The raised knee twists before the head clears; what do you change?
flashcards.answer: Do not force head clearance by hauling the foot. Reopen space with the frame and hip angle or reset.
flashcards.answer_line: Release the foot pull and adjust through the hips

plausible: Keep the knee fixed and pull the foot farther
Continue the hip turn while the head still blocks the leg
trap: Add wrist leverage before making room for the foot

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (bottom): Which body area does the supported rotation prepare to attack?
flashcards.answer: The hip rotation establishes a leg-assisted shoulder lock; a lower-body finish would require a separate captured leg.
flashcards.answer_line: The shoulder retained by the upper-arm clamp

plausible: The elbow straightened against a leg fulcrum
The wrist bent with the upper arm unrestrained
trap: The neck compressed beneath a shin

defender.description: Rotate to Carni (defender): A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below. Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control.
defender.overview:
The bottom guard player begins in New York with a safe neck-clearing angle, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Richie Martinez demonstrates the shoulder-lock mechanics through Jersey from Z guard. A direct New York entry is a positional adaptation, not established by that lesson alone.

A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below. Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control. Maintain a balanced base and a safe inside frame before the shoulder becomes clamped.

Create slack around the shoulder and elbow before moving the hips past the legs. Do not force a forward roll when the triceps and wrist are fixed; tap if pressure has already engaged. Raise the head and chest only after the arm and head-side leg are clear.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

An early escape removes the triceps and leg connections before the shoulder is fixed. Keep the arm aligned until it is free; standing or rolling against the clamp adds rotation instead of releasing it.
key_principles: Identify the shoulder threat: A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below.
Keep the elbow close early: Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control.
Deny the belly-down angle: Maintain a balanced base and a safe inside frame before the shoulder becomes clamped.
Free the arm before passing: Create slack around the shoulder and elbow before moving the hips past the legs.
Avoid rolling against the lock: Do not force a forward roll when the triceps and wrist are fixed; tap if pressure has already engaged.
Rebuild posture after release: Raise the head and chest only after the arm and head-side leg are clear.

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (top): Which combination signals the emerging shoulder trap?
flashcards.answer: Recognize the overhook and head-side leg as upper-body shoulder-control geometry.
flashcards.answer_line: An overhook plus a leg clearing your head

plausible: A wrist grip with both upper arms free
A high shin behind the head with no arm isolated
trap: A lower hook with the head-side leg still low

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (top): How do you avoid giving the triceps grip a long arm?
flashcards.answer: Keep the elbow compact early rather than reaching away as the opponent establishes triceps control.
flashcards.answer_line: Keep the elbow compact beside the ribs

plausible: Reach straight past the opponent's far hip
Post the hand behind you while turning away
trap: Lift the elbow high with the wrist fixed

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (top): What can oppose the angle before your shoulder is immobilized?
flashcards.answer: Use frames while space remains; once the shoulder is fixed, seek release rather than forcing the angle.
flashcards.answer_line: A balanced base and an inside forearm barrier

plausible: A wide floor post with the elbow away from the ribs
A chest lift before the head-side leg clears
trap: A wrist grip with the forearm outside the chest gap

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (top): What needs to open before you move around the legs?
flashcards.answer: Release the upper-body clamp before turning the hips into a separate passing exchange.
flashcards.answer_line: The triceps grip and high leg clamp

plausible: Only the lower butterfly hook
Only the wrist grip while the triceps stays held
trap: Only the head frame while the leg still clamps

flashcards.question: Rotate to Carni (top): Why can rolling forward increase the lock?
flashcards.answer: A forward roll is not a reliable release when wrist and triceps stay fixed. Obtain release or tap before moving through the lock.
flashcards.answer_line: The fixed arm prevents the shoulder following

plausible: The triceps slides free before the torso starts rotating
The retained wrist follows the torso without moving the shoulder
trap: The lower hook takes the rotation instead of the captured arm
